courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a Gaussian: position, covariance, opacity, SH color
md: Opacity is not the alpha used in blending. Alpha at a pixel is opacity times the Gaussian's falloff $G$ at that pixel, so the same Gaussian contributes strongly at its center and almost nothing a few standard deviations away.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
md: LL/SC detects *writes*, so it is immune to A to B to A in principle. In practice the pop needs a load between LL and SC, which hardware does not guarantee to support, and languages expose CAS anyway.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
md: If two stages interact, no single number per stage tells the whole story. Test the key combinations (a 2 x 2 grid for a suspected pair), and when you need a per-stage split of the total, use Shapley values, which sum exactly to the full-minus-baseline gain.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: A harness is a loop: call the model, run the tool calls it asks for, append the results, repeat until the model returns no tool calls or a budget runs out. Everything else (context management, permissions, traces, evals) is infrastructure around that loop.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts
md: Misconception: conflict resolution is a database problem you can solve with "latest write wins". Whether two facts conflict is a judgment about meaning ("eats fish" vs "vegetarian" share no words), which is why Mem0 asks an LLM. That also means the resolver can be wrong: a sarcastic "oh sure, I love meetings" can delete a real preference.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: When more samples hurt, and how agreement helps
md: Misconception: more samples are always at least as good. Searching harder against a learned or LLM verifier is optimization against an imperfect proxy, which is reward hacking at inference time. Cap $N$ where measured accuracy peaks, not where your budget ends.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: The normal approximation is optimistic for short texts. For $T = 50$, $\gamma = 0.25$ and 25 green tokens, $z = 4.08$ and the normal tail is $2.2 \times 10^{-5}$, but the exact binomial tail is $1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, about 5.5 times larger. Use the exact binomial when T is small.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Misconception: *a text's embedding is a fixed property of the text.* In a role-aware model the same string gets one vector as a query and a different vector as a document, by design. Which vector you get depends on how you called the model.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
md: Do not cache or replay a 429 as if it were an answer. RFC 6585 says responses with status 429 "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". Also note that a 429 is not always temporary: Anthropic returns 429 without a `retry-after` header when an organization reaches its monthly spend cap, and retrying keeps failing until access resumes.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: Async Rust in one breath: `async fn` compiles to a lazy state machine; `poll` advances it until an await is Pending; the waker plus the epoll-based driver decide when to poll again; Tokio's workers spread tasks with local queues and stealing; and because nothing preempts a task, every task must reach a Pending await often, or move blocking work to `spawn_blocking`.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Embeddings as features: VGGish, YAMNet and PANNs
md: Split by clip (or by source recording), never by patch. Patches of one clip overlap by 50% and share the same label, so a random patch-level split puts near-copies in train and test and inflates accuracy. ESC-50 ships 5 folds for this reason, and the TensorFlow tutorial carries each clip's fold number along with every patch embedding and splits by fold.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist
md: End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Why weight bytes set the price of decoding
md: A 1.58-bit model is not a compressed full-precision model. It is a model whose weights were ternary during training, so nothing is lost when you ship the ternary weights.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: A 2-bit counter can be fooled by alternation. For a branch that goes T, N, T, N, a counter starting at WN bounces between WN and WT and is wrong every single time (100 percent misses in our simulation). From the other start states it gets 50 percent. Agner Fog's manual describes this same worst case.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: Misconception: "a delete in an LSM-tree frees space immediately." It adds data: a tombstone. Space comes back only when compaction merges the tombstone with every older version of that key and can finally drop both.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
md: Recency alone cannot tell a hot page from a page that was just read once. Every scan-resistant policy adds some second signal: a count, a second reference, or knowledge of which query read the page.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
md: Encoder: bytes plus hashed n-grams, pooled into patch vectors by masked cross-attention. Latent Transformer: the expensive part, once per patch. Decoder: bytes query patch outputs to predict the next byte.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: A clean Miri run is evidence, not proof. Miri is dynamic: it only checks the paths your tests execute, and the Book notes it does not cover every way code can be unsound. Combine it with tests that hit the edge cases, such as mid = len and mid = len + 1.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
md: Think in **miss rate**, not hit rate. CMU's point: 99% hits is twice as fast as 97% when misses cost 100 cycles, because the misses dominate the time.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: A low CTR at rank 4 does not mean a document is less relevant than one at rank 1. CTR mixes two things: how often the slot is seen and how good the document is. You must separate them before clicks can serve as relevance labels.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: The contrastive loss on a 4 x 4 batch
md: A common misreading: the off-diagonal pairs are not known to be unrelated. Two captions in a batch may both describe dogs. The loss still pushes them apart, so duplicates and near-duplicates in a batch become false negatives. With 32,768 pairs per batch this is noise the model tolerates, not something the loss detects.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO optimizes for the inputs you profiled. The Clang manual warns that code not exercised in the profile "will be optimized as if it is unimportant". Profiling only a unit-test suite or a single toy input can make the real workload slower.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Assume the model will sometimes be wrong or hijacked, and design so that it does not matter much: isolate the machine, keep secrets and broad network access out of it, require a human for irreversible actions, and check every action before it runs.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: Linearizability is not serializability. Serializability is about transactions over many objects appearing in *some* serial order, with no real-time rule. Linearizability is about single operations on one object, *with* the real-time rule. Their combination is strict serializability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
md: Consistent hashing balances keys. Hot keys need a different tool: copies (replication, client caches) for read-hot keys, splitting for write-hot keys, and miss coalescing for keys that expire under load.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: Solvers do not escape the worst case. Finite-domain CSPs include NP-complete problems such as Boolean satisfiability, so some instances still take exponential time. What solvers do well is prune: most real instances never get near the full $d^n$.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: The state object, not the transcript, is the source of truth for what the user wants right now. The LLM proposes changes to it; code applies them; the query is a pure function of it.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Do not ask about what the state already answers, or about slots marked dontcare. Repeated or redundant questions are the fastest way to make mixed-initiative feel worse than a plain search box.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: CoT monitoring is most trustworthy where the CoT is necessary: behaviors that need long serial reasoning must pass through readable tokens. It is weakest for behaviors a model can do in one forward pass, and it stays useful only as long as training does not teach the CoT to look clean.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: Joint attention makes each document token's representation a function of the query. That is the source of the accuracy gain and the reason nothing beyond tokenization can be reused across queries.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A CuTe layout is not limited to row- or column-major, and the index it returns is in elements of whatever it is applied to, not bytes. The same function can index global memory, shared memory, registers, or even map thread ids to coordinates.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: CXL attacks two problems at once: capacity and bandwidth that DDR pins cannot scale (memory *expansion*), and DRAM that is stuck on the wrong host (memory *pooling*). Both rely on one property: the CPU reaches the memory with plain loads and stores, so applications do not change.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Excess loss: measuring how much a domain can still be learned
md: High loss is not the same as high value. A domain can have high loss because it is **unpredictable** (high entropy, like hashes), and no amount of data fixes that. Excess loss subtracts out that irreducible part using a reference model.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: SoA has real costs beyond random access. Adding or removing an element writes to every field array, the code needs one pointer or slice per field, and an element can no longer be passed around as one object. The ISPC performance guide calls hand-written SoA access syntax "messy", which is why tools like ISPC's `soa<8>` and Zig's `MultiArrayList` exist.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
md: The forward process is fixed and trivial. The only thing to learn is a **mask predictor**: given a partly masked sequence, output a distribution over the vocabulary at every masked position. It needs no timestep input.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: FreshDiskANN: inserts and deletes without rebuilds
md: Do not drop a deleted node's edges and move on. That was Policy A, and recall decayed over update cycles for every graph tested. Repair the neighborhood (connect in-neighbors to the deleted node's out-neighbors) and prune with alpha > 1.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
md: "Reference-free" also means there is no explicit KL anchor to the starting model. ORPO's SFT term and SimPO's length normalization and margin are what keep these losses from degenerating, and the SimPO authors stress that hyperparameter tuning matters for every offline method, DPO included.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Switch reads only when sustained, high-volume comparison shows zero unexplained mismatches, and keep dual writes running so the switch can be undone by a flag.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Estimate cost as event rate x cost per event. Keep the rate low (stable, specific probes; filters; sampling) and keep the work in the kernel (maps, not printf). That is what makes bpftrace usable on a live production system.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
md: A length term changes which correct answers GRPO reinforces most. Without it, all correct answers in a group are equal; with it, the shortest correct one gets the largest advantage.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
md: Event-based NILM reads each step as one appliance switching. When two appliances switch inside one sample, the switch continuity assumption breaks: the net step looks like a third, unrelated appliance, and the ON/OFF bookkeeping fails for both. Higher sample rates make such coincidences rarer but never impossible.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: Each field adds $\log_2(m/u)$. Agreement on a rare value (a domain) is worth far more than agreement on a common one (a city), and a missing field adds nothing instead of counting as a disagreement.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Closing a descriptor removes it from the interest list only when **every** descriptor referring to the same open file is closed. If a `dup` or a `fork` left another copy open, events can keep arriving for a number you already closed. Call `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` before closing when duplicates may exist.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: Resample queries, keep each query's pair of scores together, and report the interval along with the mean. A CI that crosses zero means your query set cannot tell the systems apart, whatever the point estimate says.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
md: A fix needs both size and alignment: each hot item must start on a line boundary and be at least a line long. And pad only data that different threads write often; group everything else tightly.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: Secure aggregation hides *who contributed what*. It does not make the result safe to publish: the sum of 100 updates can still reveal a rare phrase typed by one user. For that you need noise, and a budget that accounts for every round you release.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Load imbalance, routing collapse and the auxiliary loss
md: A balance loss is not a free regularizer. Its gradient changes the router toward balance, not toward predicting the next token. The loss-free paper calls these **interference gradients**, and they are the reason a strong $\alpha$ costs model quality.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
md: Two classic bugs. First, `kv_last_page_len` is never 0: a request with exactly 8 tokens and page size 4 has 2 pages and last length 4. Second, FlashInfer does not allocate or free pages. Its FAQ says page-table management is the serving engine's job; FlashInfer only computes attention over whatever arrays you pass (int32, per the docs).

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
md: Testing samples behaviors; verification covers all of them. Model checking covers every behavior of a bounded model of the design. Proof covers every behavior of the code, but only for the properties you wrote down.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: Do not copy FP16's overflow handling. FP16 automatic mixed precision skips the update and shrinks the loss scale when an overflow appears. The FP8 paper explains that overflows are much more likely in FP8's narrow range, so skipping would discard too many steps; FP8 recipes **saturate** out-of-range values to the maximum instead.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
md: `synchronous_commit = off` and `fsync = off` sound similar but are not. The first may lose the last ~600 ms (by default) of acknowledged commits and stays consistent. The second can corrupt the whole cluster and is only for data you can recreate, such as an initial bulk load.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Plate solving: finding where a photo points with no first guess
md: Stars have no texture, so a plate solver identifies them by the *shape* of small groups. The whole design is: describe shape with numbers that ignore position, rotation and scale; look those numbers up; then verify every proposal against the rest of the image.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Misconception: latitude and longitude are x and y on a flat grid. They are angles on a sphere. Any shortcut that treats them as planar (Euclidean distance on degrees, fixed-size degree boxes) is wrong by a factor of $1/\cos\varphi$ in the east-west direction and breaks at 180 degrees longitude and near the poles.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo
md: Tiling turns $k^2$ loads per output into roughly 1 plus halo, and the halo shrinks as the tile gets wider. Separability turns $k^2$ multiply-adds into $2k$ but adds a full intermediate write and read. Large windows want both; small windows on byte data often want tiling alone.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Reusing a freed block on the same stream is safe without synchronization because stream order already serializes the old and new users. Cross-stream reuse needs events: record_stream in PyTorch, event dependencies in cudaMallocAsync pools.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: **Padding by any amount does not work.** The conflict degree is $\gcd(\text{row width}, 32)$. A row width of 33 gives 1, but a width of 34 gives a 2-way conflict and 48 gives 16-way. Pick an odd width.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Low occupancy always costs you latency hiding; high occupancy does not always buy you speed. Use the `launch__occupancy_limit_*` metrics to learn which resource caps you, then decide whether that cap is actually the thing hurting the kernel.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
md: Portable rule for both APIs: never hard-code 32. In CUDA read `warpSize` when it matters; in Metal read `threadExecutionWidth` or `threads_per_simdgroup`. Write correct code that ignores the width, then tune block or threadgroup sizes as multiples of it.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: Do not estimate GraphRAG cost from the number of documents alone. Cost scales with total tokens, chunk size, gleaning rounds, the number of entities and relationships that need summaries, and the number of communities. The official docs open with a warning that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources and suggest starting small.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: The split in R1 is telling: verifiable rewards where answers can be checked (math, code, logic), learned reward models only where they cannot, and those kept short because they get hacked.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
md: A common bug is merging realtime messages instead of replacing state. With FULL_DATASET, a trip missing from the newest message must lose its prediction. Merging keeps stale predictions alive for trips that already finished or were dropped by the producer.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a 2 MiB mapping: offset bits, alignment, contiguity
md: Misconception: "the box has 40 GiB free, so it can provide 40 GiB of huge pages." Huge pages need aligned, physically contiguous free runs. After fragmentation, requests can come up short or have to wait for compaction.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
md: The duality does not make Mamba-2 as good at recall as softmax attention. The quadratic form is a way to compute the same layer faster in training; at inference, all past information still has to pass through the fixed state, and there is no softmax to pick one token sharply.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search
md: Common misconception: HyDE shows the user the generated passage. It does not. The hypothetical document only becomes a vector; everything returned is a real document from the corpus. Hallucinations can still hurt, but by moving the vector, not by being displayed.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: Opening deletes every structure that cannot contain the kernel. A real change that is 1 or 2 pixels wide (a crack, a wire, a thin new road at low resolution) is erased along with the noise. Size the kernel from the smallest change you need to keep.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
md: Misconception: "a timeout means the request failed." A timeout means *you stopped waiting*. Writes, compare-and-sets and transaction commits that time out must be recorded as `:info` unless the error proves nothing was applied (for example, the request was rejected before it was sent).

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
md: Match the strategy to the budget. Under about 20 trials, use a ranking (a heuristic, a cost model, or a curated list) and measure its top few. From tens to a few hundred, random sampling is a strong and honest baseline. Past a few hundred, evolutionary or local refinement pays off, and a learned model pays off at every budget.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Two folk beliefs ixy tested and found weak: bigger rings do not add throughput (they add latency), and huge pages inside the driver itself changed throughput by only 1 to 3% at realistic ring sizes (5.5% at the largest). That test ran without the IOMMU. With the IOMMU on, ixy lost 62% of throughput on 4 KiB pages (the IOMMU's small TLB thrashes) and nothing on 2 MiB pages, so hugepages still matter a lot.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: Training the student on the teacher's top-1 prediction alone (pseudo-labeling) is not the same thing. It keeps the teacher's decision but discards the relative probabilities of the other classes, which is exactly the extra signal that makes distillation work.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Accumulated sums favor older tokens, which have had more steps to collect attention. In the toy, every later token entered with a tiny sum and was evicted within a few steps of leaving the recent slots.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: Offload tiers are a bigger prefix cache with the same keys. A hit is the longest contiguous prefix found across all tiers; everything after the first gap is prefill.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
md: HLC gives causality-respecting timestamps that look like wall time and fit in 64 bits. It does not make clocks agree: systems that need real-time guarantees still have to assume a skew bound and either wait it out (Spanner) or retry within it (CockroachDB).

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: ColBERT and ColPali are the same idea at different granularities: keep one vector per token or patch, precompute the document side, and let each query token pick its best match.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Loss of auditability is a design cost, not a detail. Latent thoughts can be probed with the LM head, but there is no readable trace to check. Pfau et al. raise the same concern: hidden computation can drift away from anything a human, or a behavior-based safety check, can read.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
md: Pick epsilon, get a guarantee. The PGM-index fixes the last-mile search to 2 epsilon + 1 slots per level, uses the fewest segments that can meet that bound, and so its space adapts to how regular the data is.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
md: A common mix-up: these families describe the **training loss**, not the model. A listwise-trained model still scores each document independently at serving time, so serving cost is the same for all three.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
md: For pointwise relevance grades the order bias has an analogue: grading many passages in one prompt lets earlier passages anchor later ones. Grade one passage per call, as the Bing and UMBRELA prompts do, or randomise and repeat if you batch.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
md: OWASP's top LLM risk guidance says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention of prompt injection exists, and recommends treating the model as an untrusted user. Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do much damage: least-privilege tools, human approval for high-risk actions, and checks outside the model.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Capacity in sequences is roughly pool bytes / (bytes per token x tokens per sequence). Every lever (GQA, FP8 KV, more GPUs, smaller weights, shorter contexts, less waste per sequence) moves one of those three terms.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Why asking nicely for JSON is not enough
md: Three different promises are easy to confuse: *parses as JSON*, *matches my schema*, and *is correct*. JSON mode gives the first, schema-constrained output gives the second, and only your own validation and evaluation can check the third.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: The predictions in this lesson are hand-written to show typical error types. They are not measurements of any model. Use the method, not the numbers.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists
md: Every input saving has a quality price. Truncation can cut the sentence that made a passage relevant. A smaller $k$ means relevant documents retrieved at rank 31 or lower are never reranked. Measure NDCG@10 at each setting on your own queries before shipping the cheaper one.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Cascades: answer cheaply, score the answer, escalate if unsure
md: A scorer is only as good as the data it was trained on. Thresholds like 0.96 were tuned on one dataset's training split. On a new kind of query an overconfident scorer accepts wrong cheap answers silently: cost goes down and nobody notices that quality went down too. Track the acceptance rate per tier and audit a sample of accepted answers.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
md: The ratio test needs at least two neighbors, so use `knnMatch(..., k=2)`. A matcher created with `crossCheck=True` is meant for `match()`, which returns one best match per descriptor.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
md: Helping is the general trick for multi-step lock-free updates: leave the structure in a state that any thread can recognise as half-finished and complete on the owner's behalf. Then no thread ever needs to wait for a specific other thread.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
md: T3's baseline is all zeros, so its MAD is 0 and the modified z-score divides by zero. Never let a never-fired template be scored this way: handle it with a separate **first-seen** rule that alerts the first time a template id appears, or when a template's lifetime count crosses a small bound. A miner that reports a new template id gives you that signal for free.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: YaRN = per-pair ramp on rotations $r = L/\lambda$ (keep fast pairs, fully interpolate slow ones, blend between) plus a logit temperature $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, all baked into the precomputed cos and sin tables.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
md: Dynamic halting is not free accuracy. It helped on bAbI and LAMBADA but slightly hurt translation, adds a ponder-cost hyperparameter, and makes different positions in a batch finish at different times.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA = frozen W0 + (alpha/r) B A, with B initialized to zero. You train r(d+k) numbers per adapted matrix, and the model starts exactly at the pretrained one.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Replacement methods give the model something specific to do instead: predict generic tokens (WHP) or produce scrambled activations on hazardous inputs (RMU). That avoids gradient ascent's collapse, but the target behavior is defined only on the inputs you trained on.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number
md: Savings multiply, but so do quality losses. Each step (fewer dims, fewer bits) costs some recall, and the costs compound. Measure recall on your own queries at the exact size and precision you plan to serve, then use a rerank stage (next lesson) to win most of it back.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
md: Every knob in this course trades three things: memory per GPU, communication on a specific link, and idle or redundant compute. MFU is the single number that tells you whether the trade worked.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
md: A **data race** is two accesses to the same location from different threads, at least one a write, at least one non-atomic, with no happens-before relation between them. In both C++ and Rust it is undefined behavior, not just a stale read. Orderings are how you create the happens-before relations that rule races out.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: Removing a node and freeing it are different events. Every scheme in this course defers the free until no thread can still hold a reference taken before the removal.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: A subtle limit of contrastive loss: it pulls every same-identity pair toward distance 0, so it tries to squash all images of one person onto a single point. The FaceNet authors argued that a triplet loss is better suited, because it only asks same-identity images to be closer than other identities, letting one person's images spread out along a region.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
md: Report mAP alongside rank-1, follow the cross-camera protocol, and compare methods only with the same tricks and the same re-ranking setting, because tricks alone can move rank-1 by about 7 points.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: Nearly every Miles feature in this course attacks one of two failure modes: GPUs waiting on each other (throughput), or the trainer computing gradients for something other than what was sampled (fidelity).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Read the case study's reward numbers the way the report does: the nine-step moving average rose from 0.438 to 0.556 over 100 steps, but one run on one task set cannot separate that from run-to-run variation, so it is an observation, not a measured improvement.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: Cache size per token is set by what you store per token per layer. MQA and GQA shrink it by sharing keys and values across heads. MLA's bet is different: store one small learned vector per token and let each head derive its own keys and values from it.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
md: SGMV groups rows by adapter and runs all segments in one launch, so a batch can mix adapters while the base matmul stays shared. Its cost grows with the number of distinct adapters and their rank, because each one's weights must be read.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon = SGD-momentum + a post-processing step that equalizes the singular values of each 2D update, done with 5 bf16 Newton-Schulz iterations. Memory: one buffer. Extra compute: under 1% of a typical LLM training step.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
md: Every piece is needed. Keeping $1/\sqrt{d}$ attention, using plain `torch.optim.Adam` instead of `MuAdam`, or forgetting to scale `d_ffn` along with `d_model` silently breaks transfer while the model still trains. Lesson 5 shows how to catch this.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock
md: A good futex mutex makes the uncontended path pure user space: one CAS to lock, one swap to unlock, zero system calls. The kernel is visited only when a thread really has to sleep, and unlock calls wake only if the word says someone might be sleeping.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
md: Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL is not serializable. The docs warn that business rules enforced by transactions at this level are not likely to work correctly without explicit locks or the Serializable level.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand
md: A CRF changes two things at once. At **training** time the loss is over whole sequences, so the model learns which label follows which. At **decoding** time Viterbi returns the best-scoring sequence rather than the best label at each position, so the output is a well-formed tag sequence by construction rather than by repair.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash finds copies of *the same picture*, not *pictures of the same thing*. Two different photos of the same dog get unrelated hashes. For semantic similarity you need learned embeddings.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
md: Colocated means no idle GPUs between phases but strictly sequential phases and careful memory handoffs; non-colocated means dedicated pools, a network refit (NCCL by default) and idle time unless you turn on async GRPO.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Simplified model: it ignores caches, assumes perfect overlap, symmetric links and that threads can saturate their controller. Real numbers differ by machine, so measure with your workload. The *ordering* of the options is what the model teaches.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Where candidate boxes come from: proposals, anchors and grids
md: Anchors and grid cells are not predictions. They are fixed reference positions that predictions are expressed relative to. A detector with 20000 anchors does not find 20000 objects; almost all of them are scored as background.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: S3 is not just a slow disk. A disk charges nothing per write and lets you overwrite 4 KiB in place. S3 charges per request, writes whole immutable objects, and takes tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds per request. Every design in this course reshapes writes into **few, large, immutable objects**.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Counts aggregate; quantiles do not. If you want to compute a percentile across instances, regions or time windows later, you must store counts per bucket now. That single decision is why histograms beat summaries almost everywhere.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
md: Dense text detectors predict a per-pixel map. EAST regresses a box from every text pixel and merges them; DBNet segments shrunk text kernels with a learned threshold, then expands them back.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: A common misconception is that editing a `.h` file only affects the `.cpp` with the same name. The compiler pastes headers into every includer, so `tensor.h` here costs 4 recompiles, not 1.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Running exactly the tests that matter with pytest
md: Node ids, `-k`, `-m` and `--lf` turn a 20 minute suite into a 2 second loop. Use the narrow loop while fixing, then run the wider set CI will run before you push.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Answer every comment, say what you changed, fix the code rather than explaining it in the thread, and thank the reviewer. The kernel guide adds: when you send a new version, list what changed since the previous one.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
md: A CoC is not only about insults. Contributor Covenant 2.1 lists publishing others' private information (an address, an email) without explicit permission as unacceptable, and it covers private harassment too.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
md: Fixup commits are not magic on their own. If you push `fixup!` commits and never autosquash, a merge-commit or rebase-and-merge PR lands them on main exactly as they are, `fixup!` titles and all. Autosquash before asking for the final merge unless the project says otherwise.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
md: Two common myths: copyleft does not make internal use public (only conveying triggers it), and it does not ban commercial use (you may charge for copies). What it controls is the terms you pass on.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: Common misconception: "the new number is smaller, so the change is faster". Two single measurements differ almost always, even for identical code. Without repeated runs and a test, a 5% gap can be pure noise.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Trace one request: a Redis GET from socket to reply
md: Trace from the specific end toward the general one. Start at the observable string or the command's own handler, search downward through callees, and use a backtrace (or a log line) to bridge function pointers, callbacks and event loops.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
md: Do not reuse a reducer's interestingness script as a bisect script unchanged. They use opposite conventions: for C-Reduce and llvm-reduce, exit 0 means the bug is *present*; for `git bisect run`, exit 0 means the commit is *good* (bug absent). The inversion silently sends bisect to the wrong commit.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: A title and description that explain why
md: Do not write `Closes #123` on a PR that only partly addresses the issue: merging it will close the issue for everyone. Write "Part of #123" or "Refs #123" (neither is a closing keyword).

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Sharing blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write
md: A physical block may back many logical blocks. Reference counts say when it can be freed; copy-on-write makes writes into shared blocks safe, at the cost of copying one block.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: Colors carry no meaning in a default CPU flame graph. Gregg picks random warm colors only to separate neighbors. Other palettes exist (for example coloring kernel, user and JIT frames differently), but never read hotness from hue.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
md: A fence without a flush does nothing for durability on ADR platforms, and a flush without a fence gives no ordering: CLWB and CLFLUSHOPT are not ordered with each other or with later stores. You need both, in the order store, flush, fence, then the dependent store.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A pose model's output is a fixed, ordered list of keypoints per person, each with a position and a confidence. Everything downstream (metrics, angles, rep counting) is arithmetic on that list.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
md: Pre-filtering with a flat scan is exact and its cost is proportional to the number of matches, $sn$. That makes it the best plan for restrictive filters and the worst plan for broad ones.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Software prefetch: distance, hints and the kernel's lesson
md: **Rule:** add a software prefetch only where profiling shows misses, one site at a time, and keep it only if performance counters show useful prefetches and the timing improves. Drepper and the kernel developers reached the same conclusion from opposite results.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: PRMs give denser, more precise feedback than outcome checks, but they are learned models: they can be exploited by search and RL, they degrade under distribution shift, and their labels (human, MC, or judge) each carry their own noise. Use them where search or reranking pays off and keep the final-answer verifier in the loop.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Training per-slice codebooks and encoding a vector
md: Common misconception: a PQ code is a lossless compression of the vector. It is not. Two different vectors with the same code are indistinguishable to the index, and every distance computed from codes inherits the quantization error.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Twenty letters, one backbone: the design problem
md:
Two separate objects, and you must keep them apart:

- **sequence**: which of the 20 amino acids sits at each position (discrete, one symbol per residue)
- **backbone**: where the N, CA, C and O atoms of every residue sit in 3D space (continuous coordinates)

The chain folds into one preferred backbone shape, and that shape is what gives the protein its function.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
md: Create the synonym set before the index that references it. Elastic's guide warns that an index pointing at a missing set becomes inoperable and must be deleted and re-created, or closed and re-opened.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Binary quantization = sign of each coordinate, compared with XOR and popcount. It buys 32x memory and very cheap comparisons, but the distance it produces is coarse and has no error guarantee.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
md: Stored on a majority is not the same as committed. An entry from an *earlier* term can sit on a majority and still be erased by a later leader. Commitment is only decided by counting replicas of an entry from the leader's *current* term, which then commits everything before it.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
md: LLM judges are themselves models. On the WikiEval dataset, Ragas agreed with human annotators 95% of the time on faithfulness, 78% on answer relevance and 70% on context relevance. Spot-check the judge on your data, and note that context precision as computed here treats a 44-word chunk and a 12-word chunk the same, so it does not see how much noise a big chunk brings.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: Every cutoff metric hides a choice: the cutoff, the relevance threshold (grade at least 1 here), the divisor, and what to do with short runs. Two papers both reporting "MAP@10" may be computing different numbers.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
md: Polling the trailer only works if the NIC writes the message in increasing address order. FaRM notes that many NICs, including theirs, guarantee this for RDMA writes but not reads. It is a hardware property, not a verbs promise: registering memory with `IBV_ACCESS_RELAXED_ORDERING` explicitly gives up write-after-write ordering.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: Interpolation is not prediction. It never invents a position: it only blends two snapshots the server really sent. The cost is that every remote entity is shown late by the buffer delay, which is why aiming needs lag compensation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
md: Retrieval must be cheap per item (dot products over precomputed vectors); ranking can be expensive per item. In-batch negatives are sampled by popularity, so correct each logit by log p_j.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: A query plan is a tree of operators that pull rows
md: Cost units are not milliseconds. They are relative estimates the planner uses to compare plans. To see real time, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually runs the query.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: A commit is only as safe as the set of machines that had it when the client was told "ok". Every replication knob is a choice of *how many* and *which* machines that set must include, paid for in commit latency.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
md: KL regularization and early stopping limit the *amount* of optimization, which keeps you on the rising side of the Goodhart curve. They cannot tell a good high-reward behavior from a bad one. Only a better reward, a conservative reward, or an outside check can do that.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: Sync cost = bytes / bandwidth + resharding. The bytes are fixed by model size and precision; good systems avoid gathering the full model anywhere, send each rank only its shard, and keep the transfer off the critical path.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
md: Correlation is not causation, and the SRE troubleshooting chapter names the two ways this bites. First, correlated events often share a cause: packet loss in a cluster and failed disks in the same cluster correlate because a power event hit both, not because either caused the other. Second, as you monitor more metrics it becomes inevitable that some will correlate well with your symptom purely by coincidence.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
md: Pagination: in Elasticsearch, if `from + size` exceeds `rank_window_size` you get 0 results, and pages are only consistent while `rank_window_size` stays fixed. Changing W re-ranks everything, as the animation shows, so never vary it between page requests.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
md: Direction matters at the boundary: Rust calling C uses `to_result`/`from_err_ptr`; C calling Rust uses a trampoline that returns `err.to_errno()`. Ownership crossing the boundary goes through `into_foreign` once and `from_foreign` once.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: scx_simple charges `SCX_SLICE_DFL - p->scx.slice`. Its own comment warns that a task that yields has its slice zeroed and so is charged a full slice. Precise schedulers take explicit timestamps in `running` and `stopping` instead.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
md: Rising numbers are not proof that quality rose. Average response length on AlpacaEval grew from 1092 (M1) to 1552 (M2) to 2552 (M3), and length is known to correlate with judged quality. The authors list reward hacking within the framework as an open question, and note that LLMs supply both the training reward and (through GPT-4) the evaluation, which needs deeper analysis.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
md: SGLang's starting point is **co-design**: the program knows its structure (shared prefixes, forks, output formats), and the runtime turns that structure into skipped prefill and fewer decoding steps. In the paper's ablation, turning off frontend parallelism or frontend hints lowered performance even with every runtime optimization on.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
md: A road network is a large, sparse, directed graph with **nonnegative** weights. Every fast routing algorithm in this course depends on the weights never being negative.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The DFT: one dot product per complex sinusoid
md: The DFT is a matrix-vector product: $N$ dot products of the signal with orthogonal complex sinusoids. Each $X[k]$ says how much of frequency $k$ is present (magnitude) and where it starts (phase), and the inverse DFT rebuilds $x$ exactly.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Misconception: "my SIMD loop is slow, so I need wider vectors." If it streams from DRAM with little math per byte, it is memory-bound and AVX-512 will not help. Measure bytes per second against your machine's bandwidth first.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The buddy allocator: split in halves, merge with one XOR
md: Buddy trades internal fragmentation (power-of-two rounding, up to about 50 percent) for fast, simple coalescing: the buddy is one XOR away. It suits page-granular, physically contiguous memory, which is why Linux uses it for its page allocator and builds smaller allocators on top.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
md: A resumed partial sample can contain tokens generated by several weight versions. `--mask-offpolicy-in-partial-rollout` removes the old prefix tokens from the loss, but the docs note this does not remove the prefix-distribution mismatch.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
md: TopK fixes L0 = k on every token, even when a token needs more or fewer features. JumpReLU and L1 SAEs let L0 vary, so their reported L0 is an average over tokens.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: An empirical variogram from a handful of points is very noisy, and the fitted range and nugget can swing a lot with the bin edges or the fitting weights. Look at the plot, try a second binning and treat the parameters as uncertain, not as measured truths.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
md: A common bug: after a rejection, keeping the target's distributions for later positions. Those were computed with the rejected guess in the context, so they condition on a token that is no longer in the output. Only the distribution at the first rejected position is valid.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
md: Whisper is an audio-conditioned language model. The encoder turns 30 s of log-mel into 1500 vectors; the decoder generates the transcript token by token, with language, task and timestamps expressed as tokens in the same sequence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: Stack: LIFO, bounded, freed by returning, one instruction. Heap: any order, any size, any lifetime, paid for with headers, rounding, free-list searches and fragmentation.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs
md: The best direction to **classify** with is not always the best direction to **steer** with. ITI compared both on LLaMA-7B: shifting along the probe's weight vector scored 34.8% true-and-informative on TruthfulQA, while shifting along the mass mean shift (difference of means) scored 42.3%. A probe can lean on any feature that happens to separate the classes, causal or not.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Watermark = the processor's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when a window first fires; allowed lateness decides how long the window can still be corrected; anything beyond is dropped or side-output. Every choice trades latency for completeness.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, cross-attention and multiple heads
md: Multi-head attention = several narrow attention functions in parallel, each free to learn a different pattern, at roughly the cost of one wide head.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
md: b = 1 is not "more correct". It assumes every long document is just verbose. For collections where long documents genuinely cover more (manuals, books split into chapters), strong normalization buries them. The survey reports that values around 0.5 < b < 0.8 work well in many settings, with optimal values depending on the documents and queries.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: Never compare losses across tokenizers. 1.47 nats per *character* and 2.85 nats per *BPE token* measure different things: a BPE token covers several characters, so it is much harder to predict. The released GPT-2 scores 3.12 on OWT partly because it was trained on WebText, not OpenWebText; nanoGPT notes that fine-tuning it on OWT brings it to about 2.85.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: The gradient points in the direction of **steepest ascent**, and its length is that steepest rate. So $-\nabla f$ is the direction of steepest descent, the direction every gradient-based optimizer starts from.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
md: Misconception: `2>&1` *links* stderr to stdout permanently. It does not. It is a one-time copy of fd 1 as it is at that moment. Any later change to fd 1 leaves fd 2 where it was.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Static word embeddings encode co-occurrence statistics. Similar vectors mean *used in similar contexts*, which often but not always means *similar meaning*: antonyms like hot and cold share many contexts too.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: KV cache size = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes, per token, per sequence. It grows linearly with context and with batch size, and it is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT = pretraining loss + chat template + loss only on response tokens (including the end-of-turn token) + a small, high-quality dataset.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
md: Compile each `.c` file separately into a `.o`, then link them. The preprocessor pastes text, the compiler checks one translation unit at a time, and the linker joins units together by symbol name.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: Develop C with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined` on, and fix every warning. Most of the pointer and lifetime bugs from this course then fail loudly at the exact line instead of corrupting memory silently.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: `clone()` everywhere and `Rc<RefCell<T>>` everywhere make errors go away but give up what ownership buys you: clones cost time and memory, and `RefCell` turns compile-time guarantees into run-time panics. Reach for them when the data really has no single owner, not to silence the checker.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
md: `A * B` in NumPy and PyTorch is the **element-wise** (Hadamard) product, not matrix multiplication. Matrix multiplication is `A @ B` (or `np.matmul`). With two same-shape square matrices both run without error and give different answers, so this bug is silent.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Watch the **gap** between training and test (or validation) error. A small gap with high error means underfitting; a low training error with a large gap means overfitting. Training loss alone cannot tell you which you have.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation through a whole network, by hand
md: With a sigmoid output and cross-entropy loss, BP1 simplifies to $\delta^L = a^L - y$. The $1/(a(1-a))$ from the loss derivative cancels the sigmoid slope $a(1-a)$, so the output error is just prediction minus label. Softmax with cross-entropy has the same form.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: disks, inodes and crash-safe journaling
md: Write the pointed-to object before the object that points to it, and make the commit a single atomic write. Journaling turns three unordered writes into one all-or-nothing transaction, and recovery only has to read the log, not the whole disk.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
md: Noise in an average shrinks as $1/\sqrt n$. That single scaling law explains why larger batches give smoother gradients, why small evals are noisy, and why A/B tests need large samples to detect small effects.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal means lowest loss **per training FLOP**. It says nothing about the cost of serving the model afterwards, and the 20x ratio is tied to the data, architecture and training recipe it was measured on.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: nDCG@k answers: what fraction of the best achievable discounted gain did the top k results capture? It is the default when labels are graded and users look mostly at the first page.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Each stage covers another's blind spot: BM25 for rare exact terms, the bi-encoder for meaning across different words, the cross-encoder for precise final ordering on a short list. Evaluate the whole pipeline on your own queries with a metric such as recall at k (the share of relevant passages that appear in the top k results).

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
md: Tokenization fixes what the model can see. Vocabulary size trades sequence length against parameters; the regex and digit rules shape arithmetic; the training data mix decides which languages are cheap; and rare tokens can be under-trained.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: Cosine similarity and inner product are not the same metric. If your embeddings are not unit-length, an inner-product index ranks differently from cosine. Faiss documents the standard fix: normalize vectors to length 1, then inner product equals cosine similarity.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Language models: decoding cuts the tail, scaling stalls
md: Fluency is not coverage. Low temperature and truncation make each synthetic sample look better, and that is exactly why they remove the rare cases a student model needs. The MAD paper finds the same tradeoff for images: biased sampling keeps quality longer but loses diversity faster.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
md: `mmap` signals failure with `MAP_FAILED`, which is `(void *) -1`, not `NULL`. Code that checks `if (p == NULL)` misses every error and later dereferences address -1.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
md: Percentiles do not average. Server X serves 900 requests all at 10 ms (p99 10 ms); server Y serves 100 requests, 20 of them at 400 ms (p99 400 ms). The average of the two p99s is 205 ms, but the combined 1,000 requests have p99 = 400 ms: 20 slow requests is 2% of the total. Prometheus's docs make the same point: precomputed quantiles cannot be aggregated, but histogram bucket counts can be summed.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
md: Let the LLM do language: extract date strings and turn query phrases into structured fields. Let code do time: normalize against an explicit reference date, merge, clip and compare. The result is exact, testable and the same on every run.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Sequential thinking lets later tokens build on earlier ones, which parallel sampling cannot. s1 found that majority voting over the base model could not catch up with the budget-forced fine-tuned model.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Wiring learned memory into real models, and what it costs
md: Learned memory turns the state of a recurrent layer into a model trained online. You choose its architecture, objective, forgetting and optimizer; you pay for expressiveness in wall-clock time, and you still pair it with attention for exact local recall.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Demotion: reclaim that migrates instead of swapping
md: Demotion does not follow normal memory policies. The source comment says it ignores mempolicy, and in Linux 6.15 and earlier it also ignored `cpuset.mems_allowed`. Newer kernels filter demotion targets by the cgroup's allowed nodes, but shared memory such as libc can still be demoted outside them. The sysfs ABI says not to enable it on systems that need strict cpuset placement guarantees.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models
md: Misconception: a bigger or newer model will beat simple methods. On the M4 data pure ML lost to simple combinations, and on our toy series SES with a fitted alpha was no better than naive. Any model, from Prophet to a foundation model, has to beat seasonal naive under rolling-origin evaluation before it ships.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
md: An image is not one token. It is hundreds to thousands of positions in the same context window as the text, and that count grows with the square of the resolution. Every unified design is constrained by this budget.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is not a container. A container shares the host's Linux kernel and is isolated by kernel features (namespaces, cgroups). A unikernel is a real VM with its own tiny kernel, isolated by hardware virtualization.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: SIMD distance kernels: lanes, FMA and the horizontal sum
md: SIMD kernels are not bit-identical to the scalar loop. FAISS explicitly allows reassociation in its distance loops; that is a deliberate choice, not a bug. Do not assert exact equality of distances across CPUs or builds.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
